tier_reason: Every JRuby, JRuby_InDy and Ruby2 (CRuby 2.7.7p221) time in the record matches the round-1 (2023-02-28) tables of the kostya/jit-benchmarks README. The setup is fully public: <bench>/test.rb sources shared by both runtimes, run commands in tools/languages.rb (`jruby <file>` and `jruby -Xcompile.invokedynamic=true -S <file>`), runtime builds in docker/jruby, docker/java and docker/ruby2 (gcc 12.2.0 on ubuntu:22.10), and the CPU (AMD Ryzen 7 3800X), consistent with the A tiers given to php-src, cython, codon and graalpython on the same suite.

corrections.compiler_and_flags: jruby-dist 9.4.1.0 binary tarball from Maven Central on OpenJDK 19 (openjdk-19-jre-headless from apt; README lists openjdk 19.0.1), run as `jruby <file>` (JRuby row) and `jruby -Xcompile.invokedynamic=true -S <file>` (JRuby_InDy row) per tools/languages.rb; CRuby 2.7.7 built from source with gcc 12.2.0 (ubuntu:22.10 build-essential) using `./configure --prefix=/opt/ruby --disable-install-doc --disable-install-rdoc --disable-install-capi --with-openssl-dir=/opt/openssl1.1.1q` and `make -j4` (default CRuby optimization flags), per docker/ruby2.
corrections.caveats: Mixed evidence: JRuby loses to CRuby on several programs (fasta, regexdna, revcomp with invokedynamic; also matmul and nbody without it), so this is not a uniform speedup. Baseline is CRuby 2.7.7; against the same run's Ruby 3.2.1 interpreter row JRuby_InDy is faster on 10 of 13 and still slower on fasta, regexdna and revcomp (derived from page data). The shootout has no YJIT row: its base image installs no Rust toolchain, which Ruby 3.2's YJIT needs at build time. Times are measured inside the program after a 'started' marker and the table reports the best of up to 5 iterations, so JVM startup (shown in the separate 'Compile T,s' column, 1.6-2.2 s) and part of the warm-up are excluded, which favours JRuby; several CRuby baseline rows (brainfuck, knucleotide, nbody, regexdna, revcomp) completed only 1 iteration inside the time limit. JRuby uses 0.8-2.1 GB of RAM on these programs versus tens of MB for CRuby. The shootout states its programs are chosen to be simplest, single-thread and without low-level hacks; one machine, one round, single benchmark author. Found by harvesting rows from a shootout; JRuby's own README only says it can be used 'as a faster version of Ruby' and gives no numbers. Java project, not C++.

notes: All claimed numbers and the 9-of-13 (InDy) and 8-of-13 (default) counts check out against the README tables; outputs are validated by the suite's check step (tools/cli.rb check_exact) and JRuby is not on any expected_check_failed list. Metadata verified: EPL-2.0 OR GPL-2.0 OR LGPL-2.1 per COPYING, 3.9k stars, not a fork, last commit 2026-10-03 on master. Shortcomings to record: mixed wins, old CRuby baseline, startup excluded by in-process timing, high memory.

tier_reason: The Ruby2/Topaz and Ruby2 (CRuby 2.7.7p221) rows of the kostya/jit-benchmarks README match every number in the record, and the run is reproducible from public files: <bench>/test.rb sources, `topaz <file>` in tools/languages.rb, docker/topaz (clones kostya/topaz and translates it with `rpython -Ojit targettopaz.py` under PyPy 2.7 v7.3.6), docker/ruby2 (CRuby 2.7.7, gcc 12.2.0 on ubuntu:22.10), CPU AMD Ryzen 7 3800X.

corrections.claimed_speedup: Faster than CRuby 2.7.7 on 12 of 13 programs (derived from page data): fannkuchredux 0.43 s vs 4.34 s, mandelbrot 1.47 s vs 16.74 s, matmul 1.83 s vs 18.39 s, spectralnorm 1.44 s vs 17.18 s, nbody 5.42 s vs 43.56 s, brainfuck 17.41 s vs 115.31 s, binarytrees 1.97 s vs 6.75 s, fasta 5.29 s vs 18.19 s; smallest win pidigits 7.78 s vs 11.42 s; slower only on revcomp (7.3 s vs 4.2 s). Also faster than the same run's Ruby 3.2.1 interpreter on 12 of 13 (revcomp 7.3 s vs 3.67 s slower).
corrections.caveats: The code measured is not this repository: docker/topaz clones kostya/topaz, a fork by the shootout's own author (8 stars, last commit 2023-01-27) whose README says the original 'is not developed since 2016' and that the fork fixes the build on newer PyPy and speeds up 'some small things for benchmark', e.g. a faster default hash implementation; its commits include 'Optimize hash, by 8 times get/set operations' and 'Make file read operations much faster, by using stream'. Upstream topazproject/topaz (last commit 2022-06-18) would likely be slower on hash- and IO-heavy programs (knucleotide, fasta, revcomp, regexdna). Outputs pass the suite's own check step (Topaz is not on any expected_check_failed list). Baseline is CRuby 2.7.7; the shootout has no YJIT row. Times are measured inside the program, best of up to 5 iterations, so startup is excluded. Topaz implements only part of Ruby, so the programs exercise a small slice of the language. Single benchmark author, one machine, one round (2023-02-28). Found by harvesting a row from a shootout, not from a Topaz-authored claim. RPython/Python project, not C++.

notes: Numbers and the 12-of-13 count are correct; metadata verified (BSD-3-Clause, 1k stars, not a fork, last commit 2022-06-18, abandoned). Main shortcoming: the measured binary is kostya/topaz, a benchmark-tuned fork made by the shootout author, so the orchestrator may want a repo_url override to https://github.com/kostya/topaz or to keep this id with that documented; upstream is unmaintained.

tier_reason: The repo README only quotes the EDBT 2023 abstract ('match or even outperform state-of-the-art systems like HyPer') with no numbers, and the paper itself (openproceedings.org and bigdata.uni-saarland.de copies, arXiv 2104.15098, CIDR 2023 PDF) is EGRESS_BLOCKED here and has no GitHub mirror that a search found; search snippets give compile-time ratios only. The peer-reviewed paper would justify B once someone reads it; capped at C until then.

corrections.claimed_speedup: EDBT 2023 abstract (quoted in the README): 'Our results show that we are able to match or even outperform state-of-the-art systems like HyPer' on TPC-H. Snippet only (paper not opened): query compilation with V8's Liftoff is up to 7.4x faster than HyPer's non-optimizing compilation (Q12), and optimizing compilation with TurboFan is up to 6x faster than HyPer's LLVM-based optimizing compilation. These are compile-latency ratios; no execution-time ratio was visible.
corrections.caveats: Snippet only: the numbers live in the EDBT 2023 paper (PDF at bigdata.uni-saarland.de and openproceedings.org/2023/conf/edbt/paper-156.pdf, plus the earlier arXiv 2104.15098 'Fast Compilation and Execution of SQL Queries with WebAssembly'), all EGRESS_BLOCKED here, so the tier is capped at C although the paper is peer reviewed (a verifier who can read it should consider B). The visible ratios are compilation-time wins; for execution the claim is 'match or even outperform', not a uniform win. Baseline HyPer is closed source, run through the proprietary Tableau Hyper API. The repo ships a continuous-benchmarking harness (benchmark/Benchmark.py with YAML experiments and connectors for PostgreSQL, DuckDB and HyPer, documented in benchmark/README.md) and a nightly dashboard at cb.mutable.uni-saarland.de (blocked here), but no result table in the repo. Research system, AGPL-3.0.

notes: Real peer-reviewed academic system with a public HyPer/DuckDB/PostgreSQL comparison harness, but no numbers reachable from this environment; candidate for the paper-access retier list (EDBT 2023 paper-156). Metadata verified: AGPL-3.0 (LICENSE and README), 118 stars, not a fork, last commit 2025-11-11 (active). The metric field says throughput while the only concrete snippet numbers are compile latency.
